summary: Defines a number of QoS parameters reusable in Diameter, including data traffic parameters for describing a token bucket filter, a bandwidth parameter and a per-hop behavior class object.

plainLanguage.summary: This provides labels to ask for fast or smooth lanes on a network, such as how much traffic is allowed and what priority it gets.

subtitle: A shared set of building blocks for describing traffic rate, bandwidth and priority class inside Diameter messages.

tldr.problem: Different groups define their own Quality of Service parameters for Diameter, and a common core set was needed that many applications can reuse.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines Diameter AVPs for a token bucket traffic description (TMOD-1 and TMOD-2), a bandwidth value and a Differentiated Services per-hop behavior class, plus a QoS profile registry for adding more.
tldr.outcome: Other Diameter specifications can carry QoS information with these AVPs. The RFC itself says it does not describe how they are exchanged, so it raises no security concerns of its own.

today: RFC 5624 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2009. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Diameter Needs QoS Parameters
sections.content:
RFC 5624 defines Quality of Service (QoS) parameters that can be reused for carrying QoS information in the Diameter protocol (RFC 3588). The set is described as a core subset useful for a wide range of applications. More parameters may be defined later as the need arises.

The parameters are written as Diameter Attribute Value Pairs (AVPs), using the modified ABNF and the data types from RFC 3588. The RFC covers three kinds of information: a description of the traffic source (a token bucket), a bandwidth value, and a per-hop behavior class.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers asking a network for special treatment need a common set of words. This RFC picks a small starter set of words everyone can share.

sections.title: The Traffic Model AVPs
sections.content:
The traffic model (TMOD) AVPs are containers that describe the traffic source with five values: token rate (r), bucket depth (b), peak traffic rate (p), minimum policed unit (m) and maximum packet size (M). Their meaning comes from RFC 2210 and RFC 2215.

TMOD-1 (AVP code 495) is a Grouped AVP holding Token-Rate (496), Bucket-Depth (497), Peak-Traffic-Rate (498), Minimum-Policed-Unit (499) and Maximum-Packet-Size (500). The first three are of type Float32 and the last two are Unsigned32. TMOD-2 (code 501) has the same structure and reuses the same five AVPs.

A second TMOD is needed by some DiffServ applications. The RFC explains that expedited forwarding (EF) traffic is typically shaped by a single-rate token bucket, so one TMOD is enough. Assured forwarding (AF) traffic needs two sets of token bucket parameters, one for average traffic and one for bursts, which is why two TMOD AVPs exist.
sections.plainLanguage: A token bucket is like a jar of tickets. You may send a packet only by spending a ticket, and the jar refills at a steady speed. The TMOD says how fast it refills and how big the jar is.

sections.title: The Bandwidth AVP
sections.content:
The Bandwidth AVP (code 502) is of type Float32 and is measured in octets of IP datagrams per second. It is a simplified description for the case where only bandwidth has to be expressed.

It stands for a TMOD setting in which the token rate (r) equals the peak traffic rate (p), and both the bucket depth (b) and the minimum policed unit (m) are set to large.
sections.plainLanguage: If you only care about how wide the pipe is, you can use one number instead of filling in the whole ticket-jar form.

sections.title: The PHB-Class AVP
sections.content:
The PHB-Class AVP (code 503) is of type Unsigned32. It names a DiffServ per-hop behavior (PHB), meaning how a router treats a class of packets. Its semantics come from RFC 3140, and no new registry is needed. All bits marked reserved MUST be set to zero.

Three cases are distinguished:

  • Single PHB: the recommended DSCP value for that PHB, left-justified in the 16-bit field, with bits 6 through 15 set to zero.
  • Set of PHBs: the numerically smallest encoding of the PHBs in the set, with bit 14 set to 1. For the AF1x PHBs this is the AF11 encoding with bit 14 set.
  • Experimental or local use PHBs: an arbitrary 12-bit PHB identification code assigned by IANA, left-justified in the 16-bit field. Bit 15 is set to 1, bit 14 is 0 for one PHB or 1 for a set, and bits 12 and 13 are zero.

When one identifier stands for a set of PHBs (bit 14 set to 1), the set MUST be a PHB Scheduling Class. Using different PHBs from the set MUST NOT cause packets of the same microflow to be reordered.
sections.plainLanguage: Each priority class gets a short code number. The code is written in a fixed spot in a number, and a couple of flag bits say whether it names one class or a whole family.

sections.title: Extensibility and QoS Profiles
sections.content:
Different organizations define their own QoS parameters, so the RFC provides an initial QoS profile with a common set of parameters. If other parameters are needed, or these are used with different semantics, it is advisable to define a new QoS profile. A profile can also be registered as a fixed set of QoS values instead of parameters to fill in.

A QoS profile is identified by an 8-octet field made of a 4-octet vendor field and a 4-octet specifier field. The vendor field holds an Enterprise Number. If it is 0x00000000, the specifier MUST be registered with IANA. Otherwise the specifier is a vendor-specific value allocated by that enterprise.
sections.plainLanguage: If the starter set of words is not enough, a company can make its own set. Each set gets a two-part name so that nobody mixes them up.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA allocated the AVP codes 495 to 503 from the Diameter AVP code registry defined in Section 11.1.1 of RFC 3588. IANA also created a QoS profile registry for the standards-specified case (vendor field 0x00000000).

In that registry, values 0 to 511 need Standards Action, values 512 to 32767 need Specification Required, and 32768 to 4294967295 are reserved. The value zero (0) was allocated to the QoS profile defined in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: A librarian keeps the official list of code numbers so that two groups never pick the same one. The first entry on the list is the starter set from this RFC.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it raises no security concerns, because it only defines QoS parameters and does not yet describe how they are exchanged in an Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) protocol. Security considerations are described in the documents that use this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC is only a dictionary of words, not a conversation. Any safety rules belong to the documents that actually use the words.
